name: Etulo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ezenwafor-Afuecheta, Chikelu I. (2025), Grammar of Etulo: A Niger-Congo (Idomoid) Language, Vol. language is tonal

new_statements.quote: Etulo is characterized as a register tone language with three contrastive level tones and two contour tones. The level tones comprise the high tone [ ́], the low tone [ ̀] and mid tone [−] while the contour tones include the falling [ ̂] and rising [ ̌] tones. The lexeme's inherent tones may change in grammatical constructions. Two tone bearing units are identified; vowels and syllabic nasals. Etulo is also characterized by intonation as a contrastive feature.
new_statements.citation: Ezenwafor-Afuecheta, Chikelu I. (2025). Grammar of Etulo: A Niger-Congo (Idomoid) Language. Publications of the Philological Society. Cambridge: Open Book Publishers. doi:10.11647/OBP.0467
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 'The Phonology of Etulo', §2.4 Tone and intonation, p. 19 (PDF p. 33)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. Etulo is described as a register tone language (H, M, L plus falling and rising contours; rising is non-distinctive and word-final only; falling mostly word-final; mid restricted, never after L). Tone carries lexical contrasts and grammatical functions (polar questions via an intonational L at the right edge; tone polarity on TAM particles ka/le; H-triggered lowering of H verbs after the 3SG pronoun). The grammar, the 2017 thesis, the 2021 overview article and Armstrong's 1964 notes are all silent on stress/accent; none states that stress exists or that it is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: rising tone is rare, non-distinctive, word-final, and preceded by H (§2.4.5); falling tone mostly restricted to the word-final syllable/mora (§2.4.4); mid tone may be preceded by H but not by L (§2.4.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone described on citation-form words (mono-, di-, trisyllabic examples with tone patterns HH, HL, HM, LH, LL, LF, HF, HR etc.); the book notes words are pronounced differently in isolation and in connected speech (assimilation, elision, tonal change). Nothing on word- vs phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Etulo as spoken in Katsina-Ala/Buruku LGAs, Benue State (and Taraba), Nigeria — the language-level variety etul1245; no dialect split is described. Note the Glottolog record for Ezenwafor 2017 ('mastersthesis') is a PhD thesis per the SNS Pisa repository (hdl:11384/86018), and the 2025 Open Book Publishers grammar is its published revision (same author, married name Ezenwafor-Afuecheta).

sources.note: Ch. 2 'The Phonology of Etulo', §2.4 Tone and intonation (pp. 19-24): Etulo is a register tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) and two contour tones (falling, rising; rising non-distinctive); tone has lexical and grammatical functions; polar questions marked by an intonational low tone at the right edge. The word 'stress' occurs only once in the whole book (p. 44, quoting Lieber & Stekauer's cross-linguistic compound criteria); there is no statement about word stress or prominence in Etulo.

sources.note: §2.1 The Tone System (p. 134): 'Etulo is a register tone language with three contrastive level tones (high, mid and low) and two gliding tones (rising and falling tones). The rising tone occurs rarely and is non-contrastive.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. (1983). The Idomoid languages of the Benue and Cross-River valleys. Journal of West African Languages 13(1): 91-149.
sources.note: Image-only scan; only pp. 1-8 (introduction) scanned. Typological intro (p. 96): Igede has a four-level register tone system; 'All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems... downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent'; Etulo alone among Idomoid uses nasal(ized) vowel phonemes; Etulo materials 'collected in two or three hours in... 1952'. No stress statement. Remainder is comparative wordlists.

Followed by a tone-marked wordlist. No mention of stress.
